en: The Sūtra on the Former Life of Mahākāśyapa, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling at Vulture Peak near the city of Rājagṛha. At that time, within the city...

There was a powerful and wealthy brahmin named Nigrodha (translated into Chinese as Wúèi, "Without Anger"), whose riches were beyond measure; his gold, silver, and the seven treasures, as well as his fields, houses, oxen, and horses, were incalculable.

The brahmin had a son named Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja. He renounced sixty khārīs of gold and precious goods, as well as a thousand plow-oxen; he abandoned his virtuous and noble wife, whose countenance possessed the world’s foremost radiance and whose exquisite complexion was supreme. He thought to himself:
"I shall go forth into the world as an arhat and train in the pure cultivation of the holy life."
He went beneath the medicinal tree at the shrine of the deity Bahuputra and ate its fruit.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One turned the Great Wheel of Dharma; having finished turning the Wheel of Dharma, he withdrew with the assembly of bhikṣus and arrived at the shrine of the deity Bahuputra, staying in its vihāra.

At that time, as the night was turning toward dawn, Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja stood at a distance and saw the World-Honored One among the thickets of trees. His radiance shone afar and his majestic brilliance reached everywhere. Bhāradvāja then thought to himself:
"In these thickets, as the day breaks, his awesome spiritual power shines forth universally; his light is immeasurable, most exquisite and magnificent."

Within these trees, there must surely be a king of deer or a great heroic lion; or perhaps there are devas, or those with great supernormal powers and miraculous transformations—it must be so, without doubt.

"I shall go to behold him. Thereupon, Pi-po Xue-zhi rose from his seat and went to the grove of trees. From afar he saw the World-Honored One’s radiance extending for hundreds of thousands of fathoms; the patterns on the soles of his feet were complete, and he was endowed with all the marks of excellence. He immediately exclaimed:

"In the scriptures bequeathed by the seers of antiquity, it is said that there are auspicious signs consisting of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, fully distinguished. Such a one must follow one of two paths:"

If he remains a householder, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, ruling over the four continents; he will select the essential teachings and govern by the True Dharma, restraining the use of swords, staves, and weapons rather than employing them.

If he should renounce the world, abandoning his kingdom and royal status, he will become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
"It would be better for me to behold him in person.

Having spoken, Pi-p'o-hsüeh-chih went to where the Buddha was. He beheld the World-Honored One sitting with dignified majesty amidst the trees, like a great image composed of the seven treasures, his majestic virtue towering high, his faculties serene and stilled, his mind of the Way tranquil and calm, having attained the most profound serenity, suddenly pure and having crossed to the other shore. He was like a mountain of gold, or King Sumeru; like a great torch lit in the darkness of night; like a dragon in the deep abyss where the waters are cool and clear.

His body was adorned with the thirty-two marks, like the summit of the Great Mountain King ablaze with fire, like the sun rising over a mountain ridge its radiance shining everywhere, like the full moon uniquely bright among the host of stars, or like a Wheel-Turning King surrounded by his retinue.
The eighty minor marks were spread across his body, like various flowers, each opening and radiating hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light from the holy body.

When Pippalāyana saw the Buddha thus, his heart was filled with joy, as if seeing light in the darkness; he immediately approached the World-Honored One, exchanged greetings and conversation, announced his own name, and withdrew to sit on one side.
The Buddha preached the sutras for them, explaining various meanings and discerning their wisdom;

he spoke with the Buddha-World-Honored One’s edifying and pleasing words concerning generosity, the observance of precepts, and the disease of desire. He extracted the mind from its afflictions, held that renunciation is supreme, and provided medicine according to the ailment for all types of worldly distractions.

The World-Honored One, perceiving that his mind was at that moment pliant—whether it were a mind shrouded by doubt, a mind of joyful faith, a mind concerned with sin and merit, or a mind of equanimity—accorded with that mind and delivered a discourse. In accordance with the teachings of all Buddhas, he examined its root source and analytically expounded upon suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Immediately upon sitting there, he became free from dust and defilement, and the Dharma-eye arose within him;
attaining liberation in the present, he beheld the source of all dharmas, discerned the scriptures, uprooted his doubts, and established himself in the realization of the fruit.

Having received this instruction and attained the wisdom of the courageous Dharma, he immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, saying:

“When I first arrived, I gazed upon the soles of Your Honored Feet and announced my own name; yet as I contemplated the Buddha’s marks and signs of excellence, my heart leaped with such joy that I failed to perform the proper rites of reverence.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"Therefore, worthy one, from this day forward, whenever a son of good family goes anywhere,
let his mind be like the moon, illuminating like the light of the moon."
The radiance of his lineage shines with majestic brilliance; thus, son of good family, he opens his eyes and walks.
In this way, Kāśyapa, from this day forward, if there is a son of good family!
Cultivate your mind through practice, like the full moon traveling through the sky.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, from this day forward,
wherever a son of noble family goes, he shall cultivate his mind with discipline, just as the sun illuminates the world.
"That son of good family has never closed his eyes; he disciplines his mind and practices cultivation like the light of the sun, and you too should be thus.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"From this day forward, discipline your mind and practice cultivation like a honeybee: wherever it goes, it brings forth much benefit, just as a honeybee gathers the essence of various flowers without withering their color or fragrance."
"If you, son of good family!
Restrain your mind and practice; from this day forward, act in this manner.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:

“From this day forward, you shall discipline your mind in practice to be like earth, water, fire, and wind: when encountering purity, do not rejoice; when encountering various impurities—feces, urine, pus, blood, dead snakes, corpses, filth, or excrement—do not feel sorrow.
If you encounter flowers, incense, gold, silver, the seven treasures, or the five colors, do not feel joy; remain without increase or decrease.”
Noble son, when you discipline the mind in practice, you should also be like this:
when encountering praise, acclaim, peace, happiness, or joy, do not take pleasure in them;
and if you encounter slander, manifold sufferings, or afflictions, do not become sorrowful or anxious.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"From this day forward, sons of noble family who restrain their minds and practice cultivation should be like one sweeping a clean object; they should likewise sweep away what is impure, as well as excrement, urine, mucus, saliva, pus, blood, dead dogs, dead snakes, and the foul secretions of the dead. They should feel neither joy because of purity nor sorrow because of impurity."
"If a son of good family restrains his mind and practices cultivation, it should also be like this.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"From this day forward, you must discipline your mind in practice, just like a broom: sweep away what is clean and sweep away what is unclean.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"From this day forward, sons of good family who discipline their minds in practice should always walk with their heads bowed, like the son of a *māṅgalya* (auspicious) family; wherever they go, they should always keep their hands tucked inside [their robes]. Like a naked person who is ashamed of their body and does not cover it, they should live in the world merely seeking to sustain their life, and they should not proclaim their original clan name or speak of whether things are acceptable or unacceptable."
"If a son of noble family would restrain his mind and practice cultivation, it should likewise be so.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

“From this day forward, noble son, you must discipline your mind in practice like an ox with its horns cut off. Like an ox whose horns have been severed, you shall be virtuous, gentle, and compliant; you shall not covet the four requisites. You shall go to the crossroads, and at that crossroads where there are no gates, you shall risk your life.”
"If a son of good family restrains his mind and practices cultivation, it should also be like this.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

“From this day forward, you must discipline your mind in practice as follows: it shall be like an iron cauldron, and also like various lamps. Suppose there were many holes and leaks in a cauldron or a lamp filled with oil;
if a person with clear vision were to observe them from one side, they would see the oil leaking from each of the holes in the cauldron or lamp and falling drop by drop onto the ground.”
O son of noble family!
Examine the body as impermanent: it is a composite of the four great elements, with nine apertures leaking and discharging impurities; do not crave or delight in the body, nor regard it as marvelous.
Thereupon, Mahākāśyapa, having heard from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the practice likened to the moon, immediately received it, recited it, and contemplated the eight liberations.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"Go to the Radiant Tree."
Kāśyapa replied, “So be it,
World-Honored One!
He immediately rose from his seat and stood behind the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha and Mahākāśyapa emerged from those groves and went to another grove.
They soon departed again and sat beneath yet another tree, where the Buddha told Mahākāśyapa:
"Spread a seat for the Tathāgata beneath this tree; my body is exhausted and my back is in great pain."
Kāśyapa received the instruction and hurriedly prepared a seat for the Buddha, making it perfectly square.
Having finished arranging the seat, he came forward and addressed the Great Sage:
"The seat has been prepared; I pray that you will take your place."
The Buddha then finished sitting and said to Kāśyapa,
"This ground is soft, smooth, and exquisite.
Kāśyapa replied:
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
That earth and this earth—this human body now shall ultimately return to this very earth.
Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!”
All things return to ultimate extinction; one should maintain the mind in patience just as this ground does.
Now my Dharma robes are likewise soft and fine; I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion and pity, will graciously accept them.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa,
"If I were to accept these soft saffron robes, what would you wear?
Kāśyapa replied to the Buddha:
"The World-Honored Ones of antiquity have praised it, saying:
'If a son of good family wears the tattered garments of the dead from burial mounds and the five-fold patched robe, he brings peace to the devas and the people of the world.'"
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Kāśyapa!"
He is full of compassion and brings great peace and security; he wears tattered robes of hempen cloth, which were praised by the Buddhas of antiquity.
Kāśyapa! Arise quickly and bring water; I am very hungry and thirsty, and I wish to drink some water.
“Yes, World-Honored One!
he replied, immediately accepting the instruction. He rose, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and hurriedly, very hurriedly, set out to fetch water.
When the bhikṣus saw him, they immediately asked:

"Venerable sir, you are advanced in years; yet you are neither arrogant nor distressed. Having stilled and eliminated evil desires, you have entered a state of non-abiding. For what reason have you come here as a śramaṇa seeking to receive full ordination?"
Kāśyapa replied:
"Go to the Buddha and ask the Great Sage about this matter yourselves; he will explain it all to you in detail."
Then, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa immediately fetched water and went to offer it to the Buddha.
The Buddha accepted it at once; having finished drinking the water, he gave the remainder to Kāśyapa.
He immediately accepted it, placed it on one side, knelt with palms joined, and placing his right knee on the ground, adjusted his robes and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"While I was going to fetch water, I saw several disciples and bhikṣus who asked me:

'Venerable sir, you are advanced in years; yet you do not act with arrogance, nor are you filled with sorrow, nor are you deluded or false. You have stilled the evils of the four requisites and the manifold desires.'"

"I myself have renounced sixty *khāri* of gold and exquisite treasures, as well as a thousand plow-oxen; I have abandoned my wife, a jade-like woman who was the foremost in the world. Should there be anyone in the world capable of becoming an Arhat, I shall follow him and receive [the teachings] from him."
Now, my disciples and the assembly of bhikṣus have all come to question me.
At that time, I was previously at the Multitude-of-Sons Shrine, beneath a medicinal tree, eating its fruits and gourds; it was then that the World-Honored One had not yet received full ordination.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling in the city of Rājagṛha, while I was at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At dawn, having put on my robes and taken up my alms bowl, I entered the city to beg for food and saw a thousand rays of light emanating from the Great Hall of the Sun.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying among the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
When he saw the World-Honored One, I recalled my own thoughts: "I thought the sun had risen again, or that some great deity had appeared, for this night has suddenly become like day."

Then, at the hour of *prahāṇa*, the Buddha arose from his meditative seclusion; like a lunar palace emitting a great radiance, he eclipsed the light of both the sun and the moon, just as a great torch illuminates the darkness.
The Buddha, amidst the assembly of his disciples, likewise possesses such majestic spiritual power and radiance.
For the sake of the bhikṣus, he expounds the Dharma, just as a Wheel-Turning King is accompanied by his sons and retinue, so too is he accompanied by an immeasurable multitude of bhikṣus.

At that time, when I contemplated death, I did not see any assembly of bhikṣus who could receive [the teaching], nor any who could serve as teachers; only the Tathāgata was about to emerge from the world to flourish the transformation of the Way and then enter parinirvāṇa. Now these bhikṣus have come specifically to question me.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa, saying:
"There are many bhikṣus who do not understand good and evil, nor awakening and non-awakening, and who do not comprehend the field of merit."
The locus of all dharmas contains many principles and meanings; this is called the foremost.

Kāśyapa is most venerable, yet he is not conceited; he is equanimous and free from sorrow, having stilled the four requisites and the evils of desire. Having attained the supreme accomplishment, he received full ordination.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the venerable Kāśyapa and all the bhikṣus were filled with joy.
This concludes the Mahākāśyapa-pūrvayoga Sūtra.
